query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing or reducing environments, selective oxidation or reduction of Al and Ti at grain boundaries produces brittle reaction layers (e.g., oxides or hydride-like phases) that degrade local cohesion and trigger intergranular cracking, culminating in catastrophic failure of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary O2/H2 partial pressures during high-temperature exposures to control the extent of reactive-scale formation at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature anneals at 700–1000 °C, with precisely adjusted oxygen/hydrogen partial pressures and controlled hold times.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of brittle oxide or hydride phases concentrated at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Reacting Al and Ti at grain boundaries forms brittle layers that serve as crack initiation pathways, reducing the alloy’s ductility under thermal stress and leading to abrupt fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to higher partial pressures of O2 or H2 will exhibit earlier intergranular crack initiation, greater oxide/hydride coverage, and reduced tensile ductility compared to inert-environment baselines.
generation.baseline: Identical additively manufactured specimens held at the same temperatures and durations in an inert environment (e.g., argon) with negligible oxide/hydride formation and delayed crack initiation.
generation.boundary: At temperatures below approximately 700 °C or in near-zero O2/H2 partial pressures, the proposed reactive-scale-driven embrittlement mechanism should be minimal or absent.
generation.uncertainty: The precise stoichiometry of the newly formed grain-boundary phases and any synergistic effects with other species (e.g. nitrogen, residual contaminants) remain to be clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose sets of as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens to the same time-temperature profiles (e.g. 10–50 h at 800–1000 °C) but systematically vary O2/H2 partial pressures. Collect microstructural and mechanical data before and after exposure for each condition.
measurements: Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) and EDS to track growth of boundary-adjacent oxide/hydride phases
X-ray diffraction to identify phase evolution
Cross-sectional microhardness and nanoindentation to assess local mechanical property changes near boundaries
In situ or post-exposure tensile testing to measure ductility and the onset of intergranular cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no substantial correlation emerges between higher O2/H2 partial pressure, brittle boundary-phase formation, and premature intergranular fracture, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents the mechanical stability analysis of the oxide scales. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy. The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.

AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. decision.trend: Early work on SLM-fabricated FCC HEAs (PMC9414008) established how minor phases (such as nitrides and σ) appear upon additive manufacturing and evolve with thermal treatment. Subsequent reactive atomistic simulations in a related Fe–Ni–Cr system (PMC9969177) revealed how surface-oxide formation and local phase changes under corrosive conditions can degrade mechanical properties. More recent oxidation studies of FeNiCuAl-based HEAs (PMC13208696) demonstrated that multi-element oxide scales can profoundly affect high-temperature performance. Despite these advances, the precise coupling of reactive-scale formation, internal damage progression, and sudden fracture in additively manufactured Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti alloys remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear whether catastrophic failure stems primarily from rapid formation of brittle oxide/nitride networks at grain boundaries or from subsurface embrittlement triggered by oxidation/reduction reactions at elevated temperatures. The exact mechanism leading from microstructural attack to sudden ultimate fracture has not been pinned down experimentally.
decision.lever: Conduct systematic high-temperature exposures (e.g., 700–1000 °C) in situ under controlled O2/H2 partial pressures while periodically measuring crack initiation/growth and characterizing near-surface phases (using X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, etc.). Compare oxide/nitride scale formation, interfacial integrity, and fracture modes with those in baseline (as-built) samples at the same temperatures but in inert environments.
decision.why: Varying gas environments in a controlled way directly tests whether reactions at the alloy surface drive underlying microstructural degradation that culminates in abrupt failure. Prior work shows how selective oxidation and microstructural evolution can degrade mechanical response; thus, isolating the role of reactive-scale growth will clarify if (and how) newly formed phases embrittle the matrix so severely that catastrophic failure occurs.
